lessons.title: Plan and trial data collection
lessons.summary: Choose data types and a sampling plan, then check for bias before collecting more data.
lessons.objective: Choose data types and a sampling plan, then check for bias before collecting more data.
lessons.before: List what you will record and what counts as one observation.
lessons.ideas:
Categories are labels. Counts are discrete numbers. Continuous measurements can take any value within a range.

A sample should give relevant groups a chance to be selected. A bigger sample does not automatically fix selection bias.

Use the trial to fix unclear categories or wording, then choose a related question that tests your next idea.

examples.title: Choose the kind of data
examples.question:
A student plans a 6-day investigation. Their first variable is height of a sculpture.

  1. Choose the type of this variable. Options: A. Discrete. B. Categorical. C. None of these. D. Continuous.

    [2]

  2. Give one useful thing to check in a short trial of the collection method.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Measured height can take any value in a range.

Continuous

(b) A short trial catches unclear definitions before the full investigation.

Check that observers record the same variable in the same units.

examples.title: Sample a whole group fairly
examples.question:
For a school travel study, there are 28 names in the year. A student asks the first 3 learners to arrive at the bicycle shelter.

  1. Which new plan best reduces selection bias? Options: A. Use a random sample drawn from the full year list.. B. Ask more learners at the bicycle shelter.. C. Choose only learners who arrive earliest.. D. Send the question to the cycling club only..

    [2]

  2. Suggest a neutral question to ask.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) A bicycle-shelter sample can over-represent cyclists. Selecting from the full year can include all ways of travelling.

Use a random sample drawn from the full year list.

(b) Offer reasonable categories and allow an ‘other’ option if needed.

How did you travel to school today?

examples.title: Compare proportions from a trial
examples.question:
In a trial survey, 16 of 23 learners in one class chose music. In another class, 22 of 29 did.

  1. Give the proportion choosing music in the first class.

    [2]

  2. Suggest a second useful question about the same learners.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Divide the count choosing music by all responses from the first class.

\(\frac{16}{23}\)

(b) A related question could help explain the first pattern. Try both questions on a small group before a full survey.

For example, ask whether music lessons outside school differ between classes.

examples.title: Critique a chart that makes a change look large
examples.question:
A chart shows a score rising from 46 to 49. The bars start at 43, and a headline says the score doubled. The survey had 45 responses.

  1. Find the actual increase in the score.

    [2]

  2. Explain why the headline is misleading and improve the display.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Subtract 46 from 49. The height of the visible bars depends on where the axis starts.

\(3\)

(b) The old visible height is 3 and the new visible height is 6.

Use a consistent scale and label what the scores represent.
